history_of_present_illness: The illness started suddenly about 2 years prior, with legs feeling heavy and trembling, leading to difficulty walking and falling over. Since then, he has been unable to stand or walk unaided, stands on his toes, and drags his legs with a stick. There is no history of fever, pain, sensory, bladder or bowel symptoms, or disease progression. The onset was acute and the course non-progressive.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in a village in northern Tanzania with limited agricultural suitability, where cassava is the main staple food. For 2 months before the illness, his diet was almost exclusively cassava. One of his three siblings is similarly affected, and identical cases occurred in his own and neighboring villages at the same time.
physical_exam: Well nourished with normal vital signs. General examination is unremarkable. Neurologically, he is fully orientated with normal higher mental function and cranial nerves, but bilateral optic pallor was noted on fundoscopy. Limbs show spastic paraparesis with flexion contractures at both ankles and knees. Leg power is graded 3 to 4 out of 5, with knee extensors and foot dorsiflexors most affected. There is bilateral hypertonia, hyperreflexia, sustained ankle clonus, and extensor plantar responses. Arms are normal except for generalized hyperreflexia. Sensation is unimpaired. A lumbar lordosis with thoracic kyphoscoliosis is noticeable on standing.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, blood glucose, creatinine, and urine analysis were normal. Urine and stool microscopy showed no ova of Schistosoma species. HIV serology and VDRL were negative. Lumbar puncture, chest radiographs, and thoracolumbar spine radiographs were normal.
differential_diagnosis: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease), transverse myelitis, spinal cord infections (schistosomiasis, tuberculous myelitis), spinal malignancy (mainly metastases), and tropical nutritional myeloneuropathies.
management_and_clinical_course: Management is supportive, aiming for symptomatic improvement and disease prevention, as there is no cure for the permanent spastic paraparesis. The patient can walk with a stick or crutches; wheelchair use and muscle relaxants have limited roles. Surgical assessment for Achilles tendon lengthening was suggested due to severe contractures. At 6 and 12 months follow-up, findings were unchanged, with permanent spastic paraparesis. Surgery was not performed due to lack of resources and epidemic extent. He uses one stick for very restricted mobility and works as a shoe repairer.

images.caption: A 14-year-old boy from rural Tanzania with spastic paraparesis. His illness started about 2 years earlier and had an acute onset. Several other people are also affected in his own and neighbouring villages.
